approachQuestion.prompt: Two values are equal only if both are identical integer leaves, or both are lists of the same length whose corresponding children are equal. Return whether two supplied values are equal. Examples: [1,[2]] and [[1],2] are unequal; [[],2] and [[],2] are equal; 2 and [2] are unequal.
constraints: A value is either a signed 32-bit integer or an ordered list of values; lists may be empty.
The input is finite, acyclic, and has no shared subobjects. There are n total integer and list objects, including the root, with 1 ≤ n ≤ 100000; maximum nesting depth is h ≤ 1000.
Do not modify the input. Indexing a list, reading a tag, and integer comparisons take constant time.
Here n is the combined number of objects in both inputs, and h is their maximum nesting depth.

options.text: Flatten both values to integer sequences and compare only those sequences.
options.feedback: [1,[2]] and [[1],2] flatten identically but have different structure.

options.text: For lists compare only the number of immediate children, without descending.
options.feedback: [1] and [2] have equal lengths but are unequal.

options.text: Compare tags, then leaf values or list lengths. For matching lists, compare corresponding children in order and return false at the first mismatch.
options.feedback: It checks both structure and payload at the exact positions required by equality.

options.text: Materialize each full value as a separate encoding with unambiguous list delimiters and integer tokens, then compare the two stored encodings.
options.feedback: Unambiguous encodings preserve equality, but storing two full encodings is avoidable.

feedback.reason: Equal leaf values cannot make a leaf equal to a one-element list.
details: Compare tags first. Equal integer leaves return true. Lists with unequal lengths return false; otherwise recursively compare corresponding children one pair at a time. Return true only when every pair matches.

Equal leaf values cannot make a leaf equal to a one-element list. Compare tags and list lengths before corresponding children. Consume each child result immediately instead of retaining copies of all compared subtrees.
“Flatten both values to integer sequences and compare only those sequences.”: [1,[2]] and [[1],2] flatten identically but have different structure.
“For lists compare only the number of immediate children, without descending.”: [1] and [2] have equal lengths but are unequal.

“Compare tags, then leaf values or list lengths. For matching lists, compare corresponding children in order and return false at the first mismatch.”: It checks both structure and payload at the exact positions required by equality.

“Materialize each full value as a separate encoding with unambiguous list delimiters and integer tokens, then compare the two stored encodings.”: Unambiguous encodings preserve equality, but storing two full encodings is avoidable.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze method-1 as described in the revealed method. Let n and h have the meanings in Q1. Use child indices and references without copying lists. Count active call frames; exclude input and returned output. There is no tail-call elimination. No hashing is used. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair among the options.

feedback.reason: Equal inputs may require every comparison, with only one active chain of frames.
details: Equal large inputs require visiting all corresponding objects. Child results are consumed immediately, leaving only one active chain of pair-comparison frames.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Nested calls remain active along a path; their storage must be counted.
“O(n²) time, O(h + 1) auxiliary space”: Each object is processed once without rescanning or copying its descendants.
“O(h + 1) time, O(h + 1) auxiliary space”: A shallow but wide input can still require inspecting every object.
